title: Bubble wrap was meant to be wallpaper
hook: Before it protected parcels, bubble wrap was supposed to cover your walls.
peek: In 1957 two engineers in New Jersey sealed two shower curtains together, hoping to sell a textured, modern wallpaper. Nobody wanted it on their walls. Then they found what the bubbles were really good for.
lede: In 1957, two engineers in Hawthorne, New Jersey, Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes, sealed two plastic shower curtains together with air trapped between them. They hoped to sell it as a textured, modern wallpaper. It flopped. So did their next idea, greenhouse insulation. The bubbles finally found their calling as packing material.

bullets.text: Fielding and Chavannes founded the company in 1960 to sell their bubbles. It still owns the Bubble Wrap trademark, which is why other firms say bubble cushioning, and it grew into one of the largest packaging firms in the world.
An early big customer was IBM, which used the wrap to protect its new 1401 computer in shipping. The order showed the stuff could keep delicate electronics safe on the move.
Since 2001, the last Monday in January has been an unofficial day for celebrating the stuff. It started with a radio station in Indiana.

bullets.opening: The wrap that will not pop
bullets.text: In 2015 Sealed Air announced a version that ships flat and is inflated where it is used. Its cells are linked in columns, so squeezing one does not give the satisfying pop.
